4.player_action: Ask the man on the steps to scratch Hale Voss into his doorframe while he still has the name.
4.narrative: The man on the steps borrows your knife and cuts Hale Voss into the soft wood of his doorframe, saying each letter as the blade bites, then hands the knife back. The woman in the oilskin nods from her window, as if the name is safer in wood than in a mouth. A voice from the next cottage shouts that carving a missing leader's name is picking a side, and another shouts back that the boats have no one left to speak for them. The argument runs down the wet lane, louder than the tide on the pilings. Behind the shed glass, Sera's hand stays on the page, and the ink there is nearly gone. Calm the lane, and the carving may stay a mark instead of a fight, while Mara gets farther. Go after her, and you leave the name in other hands. Knock for Sera, and you might still win her as a witness before the tide peaks.

One says the guild shut the road and then hid this ford so only paid clerks could use it. Another says the lock-keeper took coin this morning and told the queue there was no crossing at all. 6.narrative: Mara's fingers were white on your cloak. You kept your eyes on her and let the ford noise stay at the edge of hearing. Heat came off the pale gravel. A flake of dry clay stuck to her cheek from the fall on the bank, and her hem was still dark from the ankle-deep run. She was not looking at the chain. She was looking at the grey wax hanging from the middle link, the same grey as the sash you had left on the steps. She tugged you lower so the packed crowd would not hear. "That stamp belongs to the lock-keeper," she whispered. "He takes coin, then tells the queue this crossing is closed. Sela knows the trick. She will not drop the chain for anyone in a grey sash." Her voice shook, but the warning was plain. If Pell read your names first, these people would take you for a pair who had paid to slip the grain tax. While you watched her, the argument on the gravel got worse. A man shoved the sagging iron chain. Grain from Sela's split basket drifted in the thin water and caught on the links. She caught the boy's wrist, snapped at the shove, then saw you staring at Mara instead of the chain. Her face went hard, the look of someone sorting a stranger into threat or witness. The boy stayed behind her legs. Nobody moved the chain. Around the bend, Pell's voice carried over the hot clay. He had not reached the bar. He called the names off the paper, yours and Mara's, and said you had run the private ford without paying. A woman near the basket repeated the names. Someone asked whether a grey sash meant the grain guild. Heads turned toward the channel you had just come up. Boots still slapped wet clay, closer than the last time you heard them. Mara was still against your side. The chain was the only thing between you and the north cart track, and the crowd now had your names. You have to decide before Pell rounds the bend and points: speak first with what Mara just told you, force a way over the chain, or pull her out of their line of sight. If they believe him, they can hold you for the tax. If they believe you, Sela may let the chain drop.

1.narrative: You are Mara Fen, a resident of Reedmouth, and you came down to the west landing because the last ferry bell did not ring. The horse-drawn canal town sits split by black water, and the ferry is still half-hitched to the near post, its chain locked tight. You need a signal the far bank can answer, or a way across, before full dark shuts both sides in. Wet rope and horse sweat hang in the cool air. Old Bram holds the grey mare's head and will not look at the canal. "She was ready," he says. "The bell should have called the east landing. I pulled twice. Nothing came back." Across the water a lantern lifts, pauses, and drops, as if someone is waiting for a sound that never starts. Hester, who keeps the landing book, stands by the bell post with empty hands. The rope that should hang there is gone, cut clean above the knot. "Don't ask me in front of Bram," she says, low. "Someone from this bank took it after the flood last month. If I name them and I'm wrong, nobody will trust either of us with the ferry again." The mare stamps. The chain knocks once against the post and will not run. You can still see the far lantern, a question with no flag and no bell to meet it. While the horse is hitched and that light is watching, you can try to get word across or force the chain. Wait until full dark and the grain cart, the people, and any answer on the east bank stay where they are all night. Hester's secret will harden into blame by morning, and the two banks will have no way to call each other. Your coat pocket still holds the small fog whistle you use when mist sits on the water, and a short coil of spare line. Neither one is the bell the other side is listening for. Bram shifts his weight toward the mare, ready to pull if you say so, and just as ready to walk her home if you don't. The cut on the post is fresh enough that the fibres are still pale. 5.narrative:
You stay on the wet planks and listen. Canal water ticks against the ferry hull. The grey mare's breath fogs and fades. Bram does not speak. His hand stays on the bridle, and his eyes stay on the bend. From the lock path a man calls, close enough now that the words are plain. "Bring the rope down, Ned. If the end is cut, we show it on this bank, not on you." A second voice, thinner, answers him. "His father keeps the lock keys. Do not make the boy the story." Lantern light slides along the towpath hedge. Two yellow circles, then the dark shapes behind them. Ned is still stopped at the bend, the pale coil over his shoulder. His voice is small and shaking. "I did not cut it. I took it after the flood to splice a barge line. The end was already sliced when I coiled it." He does not run. The cut end hangs bright against his coat. Across the black water the east lamp dips twice, the old wait-sign, and a woman shouts so the landing can hear. "Show the rope, or the grain boat stays on this side of morning." The second lamp there stays low, counting. Hester's landing book creaks in her hands. "They will take it as proof we silenced the bell," she says, barely above the water. "If they carry it off, the east bank has nothing to see but an empty post." The flood-stiff chain knocks once. Bram's jaw tightens. "I will not put the mare on that chain blind." Boots grind on gravel. The search lanterns are one turn of the hedge from the landing. Ned has not dropped the coil. The far bank is still watching for a show of rope, not a splash and not a silence. You must decide now, while the coil is still on his shoulder and both banks can still see this landing. Meet Ned and take the rope before the searchers do, and you may hang a signal the east bank can read, or lose it in a grab. Answer the far lamp first, and the grain boat may wait, but the men on the path may take the coil while you blow. Face those men and make them say what they mean to do with it, or the story of a cut bell hardens on this bank with no one to answer it.
